tagline: The one-humped camel that lets itself heat up to save water
summary: The dromedary, or Arabian camel, has carried people and goods across hot deserts for about 3,000 years. Its secret is not a water tank in the hump, which is fat, but a body that tolerates extreme dehydration, refills fast and lets its temperature rise by day rather than sweat water away.

stats.size: About 1.8–2 m at the shoulder; males 400–600 kg
stats.habitat: Hot deserts and dry scrub, almost entirely with people
stats.range: North Africa and the Horn of Africa through Arabia to north-western India; feral herds in central Australia
stats.diet: Almost any desert vegetation, including dry, thorny and salty plants
stats.conservation: Not assessed by the IUCN: a domesticated animal whose wild ancestor is extinct; only feral herds live free

facts.title: Running on empty
facts.text: A dromedary can tolerate losing more than 30% of its body water. For most mammals, losing about 15% is fatal.

facts.title: A hundred litres in ten minutes
facts.text: When it does reach water, a thirsty dromedary can drink about 100 litres in just ten minutes.

facts.title: Running hot to stay wet
facts.text: Its body temperature can swing between about 34 °C and 41.7 °C in a day. Classic experiments by Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and colleagues showed that storing heat by day and losing it in the cool night saves water that would otherwise be spent on sweating.

facts.title: Fat, not water
facts.text: The hump stores fat, not water, as an energy reserve. When food is scarce it shrinks and can lean or droop.

facts.title: Born of a vanished wild camel
facts.text: Ancient and modern DNA show that wild dromedaries from the south-east Arabian Peninsula were among the founders of today's domestic herds. Those wild populations are now extinct.

facts.title: Wild again, in Australia
facts.text: Free-living dromedaries survive today only as feral herds in Australia, descended from camels introduced there in the 19th century.

notes: No iucnId: the IUCN Red List does not assess the domestic dromedary (ADW: 'not evaluated'/no special status); the only camel assessed is the wild Bactrian, Camelus ferus. Water figures (>30% loss tolerated vs ~15% lethal for most mammals; ~100 L in 10 min; 34–41.7 °C daily swing) are from ADW. The 1957 Schmidt-Nielsen paper (dated 1956 in its DOI) is the primary source for heat storage saving water; its full text was not accessible, so the specific numbers are attributed to ADW. San Diego Zoo quotes 145 L per drinking session and a 40% weight-loss tolerance — not used, as it is less specific. Shoulder height 1.8–2.0 m for males per ADW (San Diego gives 1.6–1.8 m). '3,000 years' of use is from Almathen et al. 2016; ADW says domestication evidence dates to ~4,000 years ago. Regions: sahara-arabia, indian-subcontinent (Thar/Rajasthan) and australian-outback (feral, introduced). The Horn of Africa holds very large herds but has no matching region slug; african-savanna was not used. Images are domestic/feral animals, labelled so; there are no wild dromedaries to photograph.
